articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions policy in these areas.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new general licenses pertaining to Iran and Russia. These licenses aim to authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, providing specific exemptions for humanitarian aid or other permitted activities.
The agency also published amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to provide further guidance and clarity on the updated sanctions programs and the scope of the new general licenses.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property.

Alongside these designations, OFAC issued associated general licenses. These licenses are intended to mitigate any unintended consequences of the sanctions and allow for certain transactions that are deemed permissible under the new PAIPA framework.
The action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American innovation and technology from illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License on October 16, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela.

In conjunction with the amended general license, OFAC also updated a Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This update provides additional clarification and guidance regarding the scope and application of the revised license.
The changes reflect ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions program concerning Venezuela, aiming to fine-tune the impact of these measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. These actions target entities and individuals deemed to be involved in activities contrary to U.S. foreign policy and national security interests.

To accompany these designations, OFAC issued new and amended general licenses. These licenses aim to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions, ensuring that legitimate activities are not unduly impacted by the expanded sanctions.
Additionally, OFAC published updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to offer further guidance and clarity on the implementation of these new measures and their implications for various sectors.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action signifies a de-listing of an individual or entity previously subject to U.S. sanctions.
Designation removals typically occur when the sanctioned party meets certain conditions or when the U.S. government determines that the basis for the designation no longer applies.
This removal reflects a specific adjustment within the broader Venezuela sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism designations on October 13, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing activities.
The designations aim to disrupt the financial networks supporting these dangerous activities, thereby protecting U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
This move is part of ongoing efforts by the U.S. government to combat global illicit networks and their facilitators.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics and International Criminal Court Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics on October 9, 2026. This settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

In a separate action on the same day, OFAC designated the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated general licenses. This designation was made pursuant to Executive Order 14203, 'Imposing Sanctions on the International Criminal Court,' marking the first time the court itself has been sanctioned.
Additionally, OFAC announced a Burma-related designation removal, indicating a specific adjustment to the sanctions program concerning Burma.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This license, General License 135, authorizes certain transactions related to the sale, delivery, offloading, or importation of Russian diesel fuel into the U.S. until April 7, 2027.
The authorization comes amidst high U.S. diesel prices and follows discussions between President Trump and President Putin regarding Russian diesel supplies to global markets.
This move has been met with some criticism from a bipartisan group of senators who argue it may contradict existing legislation aimed at targeting Russia's energy sector.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations and Amends Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in activities supporting Iran's destabilizing behavior.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Iran-related General License, providing specific authorizations for certain transactions. This aims to ensure that legitimate activities are not inadvertently impacted by the new sanctions.
Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License, modifying existing authorizations for transactions involving Russia.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined Over $11 Million by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., resulting in a civil penalty of $11,662,930. This penalty is part of broader enforcement actions against the bank for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
The settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, underscoring the importance of robust compliance programs for financial institutions.
This action, alongside penalties from FinCEN and the OCC totaling over $1.21 billion, represents one of the largest enforcement actions in Treasury history.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, imposing a civil penalty of $175,015. This settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
The enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions programs across various industries, including logistics and shipping.
Companies involved in international trade are reminded of their responsibility to implement effective compliance measures to prevent sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: Individual Fined Over $1.4 Million by OFAC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $1,427,230 against an individual. This enforcement action addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
This significant penalty underscores that OFAC's enforcement extends to individuals as well as corporate entities, holding them accountable for sanctions breaches.
The action serves as a reminder that individuals involved in transactions subject to U.S. jurisdiction must adhere strictly to sanctions compliance requirements.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 OFAC Penalty
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a civil penalty of $60,764 against Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. This settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.
The enforcement action highlights the importance of due diligence and robust compliance programs for companies engaged in international business, regardless of their industry.
Companies are encouraged to review their internal controls and procedures to ensure adherence to all applicable U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
